Citation: Reichert, B.M. & Obelheiro, R.R. Software supply chain security: a systematic literature review. International Journal of Computers and Applications, 46(10), 853-867, 2024.
Verification status: Supplied by course handbook (not independently re-checked)
What it establishes: Systematic review of software supply-chain security (as listed in the handbook).
How it is used in this project: Frames the problem and the taxonomy of risks; positions this work within the SLR landscape.

Citation: NIST. Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF), SP 800-218.
Verification status: Supplied by course handbook (not independently re-checked)
What it establishes: Government framework for secure software development, including managing third-party components.
How it is used in this project: Justifies why dependency risk management is a recognised practice requirement.
Limitation / caution: Practice guidance, not an empirical study.

Citation: Jacobs, J., Romanosky, S., Edwards, B., Adjerid, I., Roytman, M. Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS). Digital Threats: Research and Practice, 2(3), Article 20 (pp. 20:1-20:17), 2021.
Verification status: Verified (live sources, 2026-10-15) - volume/issue/article confirmed on dblp; 12-month definition and ROC AUC 0.838 confirmed on the EPSS authors' research page
What it establishes: First open data-driven framework estimating the probability a vulnerability is exploited in the wild within 12 months of disclosure; reported ROC AUC 0.838 for the original model.
How it is used in this project: Source of the EPSS feature and the Baseline-2 rule; motivates exploitation evidence over severity.
Limitation / caution: Original model (12-month window). The daily EPSS scores used for Baseline B2 are later model versions that FIRST describes as the probability of exploitation in the next 30 days, so B2 is a different horizon from the 12-month labels. Record the #model_version line of each downloaded file.

Citation: Jacobs, J., Romanosky, S., Suciu, O., Edwards, B., Sarabi, A. Enhancing Vulnerability Prioritization: Data-Driven Exploit Predictions with Community-Driven Insights. EuroS&P Workshops 2023, pp. 194-206.
Verification status: Verified (live sources, 2026-10-15) - venue and pages from dblp
What it establishes: Describes the design decisions behind the next EPSS version, built by a special-interest group of 170+ experts.
How it is used in this project: Explains how the EPSS model version differs across cohort dates.
Limitation / caution: Model changes over time complicate multi-year comparison.

Citation: Pashchenko, I., Plate, H., Ponta, S.E., Sabetta, A., Massacci, F. Vulnerable Open Source Dependencies: Counting Those That Matter. ESEM 2018.
What it establishes: On 200 popular Java libraries (10,905 GAVs) shows naive counting inflates risk; 81% of vulnerable dependencies fixable by updating.
How it is used in this project: Motivates prioritisation beyond raw counts; supports 'update' as the dominant remediation action.

Citation: Pashchenko, I., Plate, H., Ponta, S.E., Sabetta, A., Massacci, F. Vuln4Real: A Methodology for Counting Actually Vulnerable Dependencies. IEEE Trans. Software Engineering, 2020.
What it establishes: Methodology reducing over-reporting of vulnerable dependencies for deployed code.
How it is used in this project: Basis for treating scanner output as an over-inclusive candidate list needing prioritisation.

Citation: Decan, A., Mens, T., Constantinou, E. On the impact of security vulnerabilities in the npm package dependency network. MSR 2018.
What it establishes: Study of nearly 400 security reports over six years in an npm network of 610k+ packages: discovery, fixing and propagation to dependants.
How it is used in this project: Evidence that vulnerabilities propagate through dependency structure -> justifies graph features (depth, fan-in).

Citation: Zerouali, A., Mens, T., Decan, A., De Roover, C. On the impact of security vulnerabilities in the npm and RubyGems dependency networks. Empirical Software Engineering, 27(5), Article 107, 2022.
Verification status: Verified (live sources, 2026-10-15) - journal details from ORBi and dblp; findings from arXiv v2 abstract
What it establishes: Using Snyk's vulnerability database, studies vulnerabilities in npm and RubyGems: npm vulnerabilities are disclosed faster; a vulnerability in npm affects a median of 30 package releases (59 in RubyGems); external GitHub projects are exposed through direct or indirect dependencies; about one in three exposures is fixable by updating within the same major range.
How it is used in this project: Supports transitive-exposure features and the claim that most exposure is indirect.
Limitation / caution: Snyk data and npm/RubyGems only; PyPI not covered.

Citation: Zimmermann, M., Staicu, C.-A., Tenny, C., Pradel, M. Small World with High Risks: A Study of Security Threats in the npm Ecosystem. USENIX Security 2019.
What it establishes: Shows individual packages and few maintainer accounts can affect large parts of npm; packages implicitly trust many third-party packages.
How it is used in this project: Justifies centrality / reach features (PageRank, ancestors) and maintainer-concentration discussion.

Citation: Xia, B., Bi, T., Xing, Z., Lu, Q., Zhu, L. An Empirical Study on Software Bill of Materials: Where We Stand and the Road Ahead. ICSE 2023.
What it establishes: First interview/survey study of SBOM practitioners; 26 statements on state of practice.
How it is used in this project: Context for SBOM generation and its practical limits.

Citation: Stalnaker, T. et al. BOMs Away! Inside the Minds of Stakeholders: A Comprehensive Study of Bills of Materials for Software Systems. ICSE 2024.
What it establishes: Survey of 138 practitioners; identifies 12 challenges in creating and using SBOMs (tools, content, maintenance).
How it is used in this project: Informs the SBOM quality checks (completeness, edges) and limitations section.

Citation: O'Donoghue, E. et al. Software Bill of Materials in Software Supply Chain Security: A Systematic Literature Review. 2025.
What it establishes: SLR identifying five SBOM application areas incl. vulnerability management and risk assessment; maps adoption barriers.
How it is used in this project: Positions SBOM-to-risk pipelines among known application areas; identifies gap.

Citation: Ladisa, P., Plate, H., Martinez, M., Barais, O. SoK: Taxonomy of Attacks on Open-Source Software Supply Chains. IEEE S&P 2023.
What it establishes: Attack tree of 107 unique vectors linked to 94 real incidents and 33 safeguards; validated by 17 experts and 134 developers.
How it is used in this project: Basis for the threat model; used to scope in 'known-vulnerable dependency' and scope out malicious-package injection.

Citation: Ponta, S.E., Plate, H., Sabetta, A. Detection, assessment and mitigation of vulnerabilities in open source dependencies. Empirical Software Engineering, 25(5), 3175-3215, 2020.
What it establishes: Code-centric method (Eclipse Steady) compared with OWASP Dependency-Check on 300 enterprise applications (78,165 dependencies).
How it is used in this project: Motivates reachability as a future feature; documents limits of metadata-only matching.
Limitation / caution: Java; code-level analysis out of scope here.

Citation: Plate, H., Ponta, S.E., Sabetta, A. Impact assessment for vulnerabilities in open-source software libraries. ICSME 2015, 411-420.
What it establishes: Early code-centric impact assessment of vulnerable libraries.
How it is used in this project: Historical foundation for assessing whether a vulnerable dependency actually matters.

Citation: Ponta, S.E., Plate, H., Sabetta, A. Beyond Metadata: Code-Centric and Usage-Based Analysis of Known Vulnerabilities in Open-Source Software. ICSME 2018.
What it establishes: Argues metadata-based vulnerability databases are insufficient and proposes usage-based analysis.
How it is used in this project: Supports reporting metadata-matching as an upper bound on exposure.

Citation: Arp, D. et al. Dos and Don'ts of Machine Learning in Computer Security. USENIX Security 2022.
What it establishes: Identifies 10 pitfalls and surveys 30 top-tier papers, finding pitfalls widespread.
How it is used in this project: Checklist for leakage, sampling bias, base-rate and evaluation pitfalls; basis of Section 'Leakage checks'.

Citation: Pendlebury, F., Pierazzi, F., Jordaney, R., Kinder, J., Cavallaro, L. TESSERACT: Eliminating Experimental Bias in Malware Classification across Space and Time. 28th USENIX Security Symposium, 2019, pp. 729-746.
Verification status: Verified (live sources, 2026-10-15) - pages from the USENIX page
What it establishes: Shows that malware-classification results are inflated by spatial bias and by temporal bias from incorrect time splits; proposes space and time constraints for experiment design (evaluated on 129K Android apps over three years).
How it is used in this project: Justifies the time-aware cohort design (features as-of T, labels after T, test on latest cohort).

Citation: Lundberg, S.M. & Lee, S.-I. A Unified Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 30 (NIPS 2017), pp. 4765-4774.
What it establishes: Introduces SHAP values for model explanation.
How it is used in this project: Planned for explaining tree-model rankings (Activity 5/7).
Limitation / caution: SHAP values are explanations of a model, not causal effects.

Citation: Jarvelin, K. & Kekalainen, J. Cumulated gain-based evaluation of IR techniques. ACM Transactions on Information Systems, 20(4), 422-446, 2002.
Verification status: Verified (live sources, 2026-10-15) - volume, pages and DOI confirmed
What it establishes: Defines cumulated-gain metrics including NDCG.
How it is used in this project: Planned ranking metric alongside Top-k recall (Activity 7).
Limitation / caution: Designed for graded relevance; with binary labels NDCG reduces to a rank-discounted hit measure.
